concepts.name: Null and alternative hypotheses
concepts.summary: State a research question as a null hypothesis of no effect and an alternative hypothesis describing the effect being looked for.

concepts.name: Sample versus population claims
concepts.summary: Explain that a test uses a sample to judge a claim about a population, so the result carries uncertainty.

concepts.name: Test statistic
concepts.summary: Describe a test statistic as a number summarising how far the sample result lies from what the null hypothesis predicts.

concepts.name: P-value meaning
concepts.summary: Interpret a p-value as how probable data at least this extreme would be if the null hypothesis were true.

concepts.name: Significance level alpha
concepts.summary: Recall that alpha is a threshold chosen in advance, often 0.05, against which the p-value is compared.

concepts.name: Reject or fail to reject
concepts.summary: Turn a p-value and alpha into a decision to reject or not reject the null hypothesis, worded correctly.

misconceptions.text: The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Failing to reject the null hypothesis proves the null hypothesis is true.
A result with p below 0.05 proves the effect is real and important.

concepts.name: One-tailed versus two-tailed tests
concepts.summary: Choose a one- or two-sided alternative from the question asked and compute the matching p-value.

concepts.name: Type I and Type II errors
concepts.summary: Distinguish rejecting a true null from missing a false null and relate each to alpha and beta.

concepts.name: One-sample z-test with known sigma
concepts.summary: Run a z-test for a mean when the population standard deviation is known, computing the z statistic and its p-value.

concepts.name: One-sample t-test for unknown sigma
concepts.summary: Test a mean against a hypothesised value when the standard deviation is estimated, using the t statistic and degrees of freedom.

concepts.name: Critical values and rejection regions
concepts.summary: Find the cutoff for a given alpha and decide by checking whether the test statistic falls in the rejection region.

concepts.name: Test for a proportion
concepts.summary: Test a sample proportion against a claimed population proportion using the normal approximation.

concepts.name: Confidence interval link
concepts.summary: Explain that a two-sided test at alpha agrees with whether the hypothesised value lies inside the (1-alpha) confidence interval.

misconceptions.text: A one-tailed test can be chosen after seeing which direction the data went.
Alpha is the probability that the null hypothesis is true when we reject it.
A z-test is appropriate whenever the sample is large, even when the standard deviation has been estimated from the data.

concepts.name: Two-sample t-tests
concepts.summary: Compare the means of two independent groups, choosing pooled or Welch variants and computing the statistic correctly.

concepts.name: Paired t-test
concepts.summary: Analyse before-after or matched data by testing the mean of the within-pair differences.

concepts.name: Chi-square test of independence
concepts.summary: Compute expected counts from a contingency table and test whether two categorical variables are associated.

concepts.name: Chi-square goodness of fit
concepts.summary: Compare observed category counts with those expected under a specified distribution.

concepts.name: Test assumptions and diagnostics
concepts.summary: Check independence, normality, equal variance and expected-count conditions and judge when they are violated.

concepts.name: Effect size measures
concepts.summary: Separate statistical from practical significance by quantifying the magnitude of an effect.

concepts.name: Statistical power
concepts.summary: Analyse how sample size, effect size, alpha and variability determine the chance of detecting a real effect.

concepts.name: Choosing the appropriate test
concepts.summary: Select a test from the data type, number of groups, pairing and the question asked.

misconceptions.text: An independent two-sample t-test is fine for before-and-after measurements on the same subjects.
A significant chi-square test shows that one variable causes the other.
A tiny p-value means the effect is large.

concepts.name: ANOVA and F-test
concepts.summary: Compare more than two group means by partitioning variance and interpreting the F statistic.

concepts.name: Multiple comparisons correction
concepts.summary: Evaluate how many tests inflate false positives and choose a correction such as Bonferroni or FDR control.

concepts.name: Post-hoc pairwise testing
concepts.summary: Follow a significant ANOVA with controlled pairwise comparisons to locate which groups differ.

concepts.name: Nonparametric alternatives
concepts.summary: Judge when rank-based tests are preferable to t-tests given outliers, skew or ordinal data.

concepts.name: Permutation and bootstrap tests
concepts.summary: Build a null distribution by resampling to test hypotheses without relying on parametric assumptions.

concepts.name: Power analysis and sample size
concepts.summary: Plan a study by determining the sample size needed for a target power given an expected effect size.

concepts.name: P-hacking and researcher degrees of freedom
concepts.summary: Evaluate how flexible analysis choices and selective reporting invalidate p-values.

concepts.name: Equivalence and non-inferiority testing
concepts.summary: Test whether an effect is small enough to be negligible rather than merely not significant.

misconceptions.text: Running several t-tests between all pairs of groups is equivalent to a single ANOVA.
Nonparametric tests make no assumptions at all and are always safer than t-tests.
A non-significant result shows two treatments are equivalent.

concepts.name: Neyman-Pearson versus Fisher frameworks
concepts.summary: Critique the hybrid null hypothesis significance testing practice by contrasting Fisher's evidential p-values with Neyman-Pearson error-rate decisions.

concepts.name: Bayesian alternatives to testing
concepts.summary: Evaluate Bayes factors and posterior inference against frequentist tests for answering what the data say about a hypothesis.

concepts.name: Sequential and adaptive testing
concepts.summary: Design experiments with interim looks that keep error rates valid, using alpha-spending or sequential methods.

concepts.name: Replication and meta-analytic evidence
concepts.summary: Assess how publication bias, low power and replication results affect the credibility of significant findings.

concepts.name: Likelihood ratio, Wald and score tests
concepts.summary: Compare the large-sample tests derived from the likelihood and decide which suits a given model.

concepts.name: Robust testing under violated assumptions
concepts.summary: Design analyses that keep valid error rates under dependence, unequal variance or non-normality, verified by simulation.

concepts.name: Pre-registration and analysis planning
concepts.summary: Create a pre-specified analysis and testing protocol that separates confirmatory from exploratory inference.

misconceptions.text: Peeking at interim results and stopping once p drops below 0.05 is harmless as long as the final p-value is reported.
A Bayes factor and a p-value measure the same thing and always lead to the same conclusion.
